newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: U.N. tribunal steps up search for Croat militiaman.
newsitem.headline: U.N. tribunal steps up search for Croat militiaman.

text.p: A U.N. war crimes tribunal issued an international arrest warrant on Friday for Ivica Rajic, a Bosnian Croat militia leader charged with complicity in the 1993 murder of Moslem civilians in the village of Stupni Do.

The move followed a so-called Rule 61 hearing in The Hague last April during which testimony from survivors of the massacre was given. They said Croat forces razed the remote Moslem village in central Bosnia, killing at least 16 civilians and forcing the survivors to flee.

The criminal tribunal for former Yugoslavia's Rule 61 proceedings are not a trial in absentia but allow prosecutors to present evidence against those charged as war criminals but not arrested with a view to confirming charges and issuing an international arrest warrant.

Rajic, charged in August 1995 with leading the attack on Stupni Do, has remained at large despite a local warrant for his arrest. Media reports say he has been living in a luxury bungalow owned by the Croatian Defence Ministry and continues to work in central Bosnia.

War crimes investigator Ehsan Bajwa told the April hearing that survivors he had interviewed had described how Croatian Defence Council (HVO) soldiers attacked the village and committed atrocities against its inhabitants.
He said one woman and her teenage son had been forced to watch as her husband and two other men were shot dead. Another man's throat had been cut before he was shot.

"The trial chamber finds that there are reasonable grounds for believing that Rajic committed...wilful killing of civilians in the village of Stupni Do, (...) and the wanton destruction and devastation of Stupni Do unjustified by military necessity," judge Gabrielle Kirk McDonald said.
The tribunal presented the decision against Rajic as a breakthrough in terms of establishing Croatia's direct involvement in the Bosnian war.

"Evidence submitted in this case establishes reasonable grounds for believing that the Bosnian Croats were agents of Croatia in clashes with the Bosnian government...that Croatia provided financial support for the Bosnian Croats, particularly for the purchase of arms," it said in a statement.
Kirk McDonald also said that the failure to arrest Rajic was due to the non-cooperation with the tribunal of Zagreb and the Moslem-Croat Bosnia Federation.

The international arrest warrant will be sent to all U.N. members and the NATO-led peacekeeping force (IFOR) in Bosnia obliging them to detain Rajic -- also known as Viktor Andric -- if he comes within their jurisdiction.
Rajic, 38, is one of 18 Croats charged with war crimes by the U.N. tribunal, which has also indicted 54 Serbs and three Moslems. It has seven suspects in its custody in The Hague.
